THOUGHT: The patient has a chronic, year-long pruritic rash involving the face, upper body and arms with hypopigmented macules that are anesthetic to light touch/temperature/pinprick — one of the cardinal features of leprosy (Hansen disease). Additional supportive findings include peripheral nerve dysfunction (reduced sensory nerve action potentials in the ulnar nerves and mild grip weakness), loss of eyebrows/eyelashes (madarosis, classically seen in multibacillary disease), and skin biopsy showing chronic inflammatory changes consistent with leprosy. A positive anti–PGL-1 antibody test (phenolic glycolipid-1) strongly supports infection with Mycobacterium leprae and is more commonly positive in multibacillary/lepromatous forms. Together these clinical, electrophysiologic, serologic, and histologic data point to leprosy of the multibacillary (lepromatous) type rather than a purely paucibacillary/tuberculoid form.

DIAGNOSIS: Multibacillary (lepromatous) leprosy (Hansen disease)
